issues.item: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident in a combat pilot, the threat profile should more plausibly center on accident recurrence, mechanical failure, bodily vulnerability, or generalized hypervigilance. 'Watching others closely for signs that they might harm me' implies an interpersonal assault/paranoia-like threat that is not supported by the trauma type or by the other selected items.

issues.item: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal set otherwise reflects post-traumatic identity disruption and emotional numbing ('Lost Emotions', 'Identity Loss'). 'I feel like an object, not like a person' is comparatively more characteristic of interpersonal violation or severe dissociation/depersonalization. In this profile it sits awkwardly with the accident trauma and with the other appraisal items, reducing thematic coherence of the node.

vignette:
Rangi Parata had spent thirty years reading the sky. As a combat pilot, he had learned to process threat at speeds most people could not imagine - a flicker of movement at the edge of his peripheral vision, a change in engine tone, a shadow that did not belong. That particular competence had kept him alive through two deployments and more training accidents than he cared to count. What it had not prepared him for was the morning eighteen months ago when his aircraft suffered a catastrophic hydraulic failure during a routine training sortie over the Pacific, and the sky he had always trusted became something that wanted to kill him. The aircraft entered an uncontrolled roll at altitude. For four minutes - an interval that Rangi now describes as both instantaneous and endless - he fought the controls while the ocean and the horizon exchanged places repeatedly through his canopy. He managed a partial recovery and ejected at dangerously low altitude, sustaining spinal compression injuries on landing. He survived. His co-pilot did not.

In the weeks that followed, as Rangi recovered in hospital and then at home, something that had once felt solid in him began to give way. He had always understood himself through the lens of his vocation - the steadiness, the technical mastery, the capacity to remain functional under extreme pressure. Now he sat in his living room in San Diego and felt like a stranger wearing his own face. He had come to believe, with a quiet and terrible certainty, that whatever the accident had taken from him was not coming back. The man who had walked onto that flight deck was gone, and what remained was permanently altered - diminished in some way he could not precisely name but felt constantly. He noticed that he could not access emotions that had once come easily: tenderness toward his wife, Mere, satisfaction after a good meal, the mild pleasure of an evening on the back porch. These were not merely muted; they felt inaccessible, as though the circuitry had been burned out. He was certain he would never feel normal again.

It was this conviction - that he was now a fundamentally damaged and unpredictable version of himself - that fed directly into how he moved through the world. Because Rangi no longer trusted his own responses or his own judgment, he compensated by treating every environment as a potential emergency. If the man he had been could not be relied upon, then the environment had to be controlled instead. At restaurants with Mere, he would position himself with his back to the wall and spend the first several minutes cataloguing exits - the front door, the kitchen corridor, the fire escape visible through a side window - before he could settle enough to read the menu. At home, which had once been a place of straightforward ease, he remained on guard in a way that exhausted him and bewildered his wife. He checked the locks repeatedly before bed, sat facing doorways, and startled badly at sounds that registered to anyone else as ordinary - a car backfiring two streets away, the particular pitch of a smoke alarm in a neighbouring apartment. His hypervigilance was not, in his own accounting, irrational; it was the logical response of a man who no longer believed he could trust his own capacity to cope if something went wrong. The threat monitoring was, in a sense, the only remaining competence he felt confident claiming.

Over eighteen months this had narrowed his life considerably. He had been placed on extended medical leave, and the squadron environment - the sound of jet engines, the sight of flight suits, the specific quality of early-morning light on a tarmac - had become impossible to approach without a flooding sense of danger he could not modulate. His marriage, though intact, had grown strained under the weight of his guardedness and his emotional unavailability. Mere had begun to describe herself, gently but unmistakably, as lonely.

What finally brought Rangi to the clinic was a conversation with his commanding officer about a possible return to administrative duties. The prospect of re-entering that world - not the cockpit, just the building - had produced a fear so acute it frightened him. What he hopes for, he said in the intake session, is to recognise himself again. What he is most afraid of is that there is no longer anyone there to recognise.
